n: Passover comes first among the yearly feasts. It was held in the spring month of Abib to remember the night God brought Israel out of Egypt.

f.g: “Month of fresh grain ears” (March–April); later called Nisan.

n: Passover sacrifices were to be offered at the central sanctuary. Christians see in the Passover lamb a type of Jesus Christ, sacrificed for us.
For seven days they ate flat bread without yeast — “bread of affliction” — recalling their hurried escape when there was no time to let dough rise.
No yeast anywhere in their territory for the week, and none of the Passover meat could be left until morning.

f.g: Bread made with yeast; leaven often symbolizes corruption.

n: Passover could no longer be sacrificed in each home town as in Egypt; it must be at the chosen place.
The sacrifice was made at sunset, the very time of day Israel had left Egypt.

f.w: at even, at the going down of the sun

n: The lamb was cooked and eaten at the sanctuary; next morning the worshipers returned to their lodgings.

f.g: Hebrew literally “boil” or “cook”; Exodus 12:9 specifies roasting with fire.

n: The week ended with a holy gathering on the seventh day, a day of rest from work.
The second feast was counted seven weeks from the start of grain harvest. Its later Greek name, Pentecost, means “fiftieth.”

f.w: put the sickle to the corn

n: The Feast of Weeks celebrated the wheat harvest. Each person brought a voluntary gift in proportion to how God had blessed them.
Everyone celebrated together — family, servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows. Gratitude was meant to be shared.
Remembering slavery in Egypt kept Israel humble and generous toward the vulnerable.

f.w: thou wast a bondman in Egypt

n: The third feast, Tabernacles, came in the fall after the grain and grapes were gathered. Families lived in leafy booths, recalling the wilderness years.
Again, the whole community rejoices — including those who might otherwise be left out.
A full week of celebration at the sanctuary, because God blesses the harvest and all their labor. Joy is commanded!
Three pilgrim feasts each year required the men to appear at the sanctuary, and none should come empty-handed.

f.w: they shall not appear before the LORD empty

n: Gifts were measured by ability and blessing, not a fixed price. God asks according to what we have.
Now Moses turns to government. Every town needed judges and officials to administer fair justice.

f.g: Courts were often held at the city gate.

n: Three rules for judges: don’t twist justice, don’t play favorites, and don’t accept bribes — because bribes blind even wise people.

f.w: a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise

n: “Justice, justice shall you pursue” — the Hebrew repeats the word for emphasis. Living in the land depended on a just society.
No sacred trees or Asherah poles next to the Lord’s altar. Israel must not mix pagan symbols into true worship.

f.g: Hebrew asherah — a pole or tree honoring the goddess Asherah.

n: Nor any standing stone pillar used in Canaanite worship. The Lord hates such counterfeit worship.

f.g: Hebrew matsevah — a sacred standing stone.
